$comment: Every texture of the Sun and the planets, and every other image under public/assets/textures/ that is neither a moon's surface (data/moon-surfaces.json) nor a ring strip (data/rings/). `sources` give the credit and licence (src/data/credits.json is built from them for the help page), `textures` map a public path to how `pnpm gen:surfaces` makes it: a real `map` (read, turned so the prime meridian is at the centre, then kept as published, coloured along `hue`/`darkHue` at the brightness of `albedo` or `level`, or made a mask with `below`), or `painted` from a recipe, with a `basis` saying what the painting rests on. `veiled` marks a world whose ground is hidden in visible light. `pnpm build:data` stops if a Sun or planet texture is missing here. See docs/ARCHITECTURE.md, "Planet textures".

sdo-aia304.title: SDO/AIA 304 Å synoptic map, Carrington rotation 2285 (June 2024)
sdo-aia304.credit: NASA/SDO and the AIA science team
sdo-aia304.note: The Sun in extreme ultraviolet light (30.4 nm), a month near the 2024 solar maximum: the bright patches are active regions. Coloured orange, as SDO shows this light; to the eye the Sun is an almost featureless white disc.

usgs-mercury.title: Mercury MESSENGER MDIS global basemap (BDR)
usgs-mercury.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Carnegie Institution of Washington (MESSENGER MDIS); mosaic distributed by USGS Astrogeology
usgs-mercury.note: A grey mosaic, coloured by us in Mercury's faintly brownish grey, about as bright as the Moon's map (Mercury reflects slightly more light than the Moon).

usgs-mercury-relief.title: Mercury MESSENGER global DEM, colour shaded relief (2 km)
usgs-mercury-relief.credit: NASA/JHUAPL/CIW (MESSENGER); elevation model and relief by USGS Astrogeology
usgs-mercury-relief.note: Colours show height (blue low, red and white high), not what the eye sees.

usgs-venus-relief.title: Venus Magellan global C3-MDIR colorized topographic mosaic (6.6 km)
usgs-venus-relief.credit: NASA/JPL (Magellan radar); mosaic by USGS Astrogeology
usgs-venus-relief.note: The ground under the clouds as radar sees it, coloured by height. It is the Terrain view of Venus in the dictionary.

nasa-blue-marble.title: Blue Marble Next Generation, July 2004, with topography and bathymetry
nasa-blue-marble.note: Darks lifted (gamma 0.42, a touch more blue) so the deep oceans stay blue, not black, on a projector.

nasa-black-marble.title: Earth at Night (Black Marble 2016)
nasa-black-marble.credit: NASA Earth Observatory (Joshua Stevens), Suomi NPP VIIRS data from Miguel Román, NASA GSFC

nasa-clouds.title: Blue Marble clouds
nasa-clouds.credit: NASA Goddard Space Flight Center (Reto Stöckli, Robert Simmon), MODIS

nasa-topography.title: Topography (GEBCO 2008 land elevation)
nasa-topography.credit: NASA Earth Observatory (Reto Stöckli), from GEBCO and SRTM elevation data
nasa-topography.note: Also gives Earth's Oceans view: everything at sea level or below.

usgs-mars.title: Mars Viking MDIM 2.1 colour mosaic, recoloured by NASA Ames
usgs-mars.credit: NASA/JPL (Viking Orbiters); MDIM 2.1 mosaic by USGS Astrogeology; colour by NASA Ames Research Center
usgs-mars.note: Published colours white-balanced a little warmer (they are too blue for Mars's butterscotch).

usgs-mars-relief.title: Mars MGS MOLA global colour shaded relief
usgs-mars-relief.credit: NASA/JPL/GSFC (Mars Global Surveyor, MOLA); relief by USGS Astrogeology
usgs-mars-relief.note: Colours show height (blue low, red and white high), not what the eye sees.

pia07782.title: Cassini's best maps of Jupiter: cylindrical map (PIA07782)
pia07782.note: Jupiter in December 2000. Its bands and storms drift and change, so today's Jupiter looks a little different.

usgs-vesta.title: Vesta Dawn FC global mosaic (DLR)
usgs-vesta.credit: NASA/JPL-Caltech/UCLA/MPS/DLR/IDA (Dawn Framing Camera); mosaic by DLR, distributed by USGS Astrogeology
usgs-vesta.note: A grey mosaic, coloured by us.

usgs-pluto.title: Pluto New Horizons LORRI/MVIC global mosaic (300 m)
usgs-pluto.credit: NASA/Johns Hopkins University Applied Physics Laboratory/Southwest Research Institute (New Horizons); mosaic by USGS Astrogeology and the New Horizons team
usgs-pluto.note: A grey mosaic, coloured by us from Sputnik Planitia's pale cream to Cthulhu's dark red-brown. New Horizons saw only the northern half well; the rest is filled in to match. Turned by 180 degrees for the app's north-side pole (see scripts/lib/iau.ts).

orbitalia-painted-bands.title: Painted cloud bands
orbitalia-painted-bands.credit: Orbitalia contributors (scripts/lib/paint.ts), after Cassini, Voyager 2 and Hubble photographs
orbitalia-painted-bands.note: Not a photograph: there is no openly licensed global map of these planets, so their bands, colours and storms are painted after spacecraft photographs (each texture's basis is in data/planet-textures.json).

/assets/textures/venus/venus.jpg.basis: Venus in visible light (Mariner 10, MESSENGER and Galileo flyby colour images): a pale yellowish-white cloud deck, faintly darker towards the poles, reflecting about 70 % of sunlight. The cloud patterns seen in ultraviolet photographs are left out, because the eye does not see them.

/assets/textures/saturn/saturn.jpg.basis: Cassini natural-colour images (2004–2017): a butterscotch equatorial zone, tan belts and paler zones at the latitudes Cassini measured, greyer polar regions and the dark edge of the north polar hexagon at about 77° N.

/assets/textures/uranus/uranus.jpg.basis: Voyager 2 (1986) and Hubble images in true colour (Irwin et al. 2024): a pale greenish-cyan ball, almost featureless, a little brighter towards the poles.

/assets/textures/neptune/neptune.jpg.basis: Voyager 2 images of 1989, in true colour (Irwin et al. 2024: a paler blue than the famous enhanced pictures): a dark southern belt with the Great Dark Spot and its bright companion clouds at 22° S, the fast bright "Scooter" at 42° S, the small dark spot D2 with its bright core at 55° S, and high white cloud streaks in the north. The Great Dark Spot has since faded; Hubble has seen new dark spots come and go.

/assets/textures/asteroid.jpg.for: #23: stand-in surface for small bodies without a map of their own
/assets/textures/asteroid.jpg.basis: A generic rocky asteroid: grey, cratered, reflecting about 15 % of sunlight (typical of stony S-type and many C-type asteroids lies between 5 and 25 %).

/assets/textures/asteroid_dark.jpg.basis: A comet nucleus: among the darkest surfaces in the solar system, reflecting about 4 % of sunlight (Halley, Borrelly, 67P).
